title: A Herbal of the Resonant Reach, with Corrections
author: Barnabas Yewdale, physician, of Greenroot; annotated in pencil by Prue Gorse, herb-woman, late of Greenroot
origin: Printed at Oakhaven; annotated at Oakhaven
summary: An old physician's herbal of orchard, Flume and hedgerow, and the Greenroot herb-woman who has spent two years telling him in the margins exactly where he is wrong.
text: A HERBAL OF THE RESONANT REACH. Being the Plants of Orchard, Flume and Hedgerow, their Virtues and their Seasons, set down for the Use of Households. By Barnabas Yewdale, Physician, of Greenroot. Printed at Oakhaven, 391 SR.

In pencil, across the title page: Prue Gorse, late of Greenroot, her book now. Yewdale was my grandmother's doctor, and she said he never once washed his hands. He is right about willow and wrong about most of the rest, and since the quarry he is wrong about all of it. I have marked him. Read the margins first. P.G., the back-end of 418.

From the preface: The Reach is the kindest country in the Octave to a physician, for here the law of Growth is our partner. A wound in the Reach wishes to close. A bone wishes to knit. The physician's whole art in this province is to stand aside and let the country do its work, and to add, at the proper season, the herbs set down hereafter.

Margin: Stand aside. That is exactly what you must not do any more. The country does its work now whether you want it or not, and its work is more. A wound closes over the splinter in it. Two cut fingers bound together will heal into one finger. Clean everything twice before you let it close, and then watch it, because it will not stop when it ought.

SILVER WILLOW. The bark of the silver willow, which grows along the Flume below the lower lock and in great plenty in the Spectral Woods. Peel it in spring, dry it in the shade, steep it a quarter hour. For fevers, the aching of the joints, and the headache that follows a long singing. Bitter. The bitterness is the virtue.

Margin: Right. Still right. The only page in this book I would sell you. Bettany puts it in her tonic with honey and raw egg, and when there is no egg, which is always, she puts in more honey and says nothing. Peel it from the north side of the tree. Do not ask me why. My mother did.

SWEET REED-PITH. The white pith of the reed that grows in the margin of the Flume, called by children sweet-reed. Boiled in milk, it is given to Cantors in the orchard schools before a long tending, and to infants for the croup.

Margin: Boiled in milk. There has been no milk worth the name since the Cascade; it turns before it is out of the pail. Chew it raw. It eases a throat, and I will tell you something Yewdale never knew, because in his day nobody needed to: it steadies a person who is frightened of their own quiet. You keep chewing, and you keep making a small wet sound, and a small sound is what we all live in now. Give it to the night-hummers. Give it to anyone who has to sit up with the dying.

RESONANT MOSS. The green moss of the humming stones, which shivers when it is touched and takes the note of whatever it grows on. Laid on as a poultice, it draws a wound together in a night. The Reach's chief gift to physic.

Margin: In a night. It drew Jem Cutler's thigh together round a nail he had not told anyone was in it, and he walked on that nail till midsummer. Do not lay moss on anything you have not opened, cleaned and looked into with a lamp. I would strike this page out entirely if the Grafters did not buy the stuff from me by the sack.
KNITBONE, or comfrey. The root grated and bound about a broken limb, which it knits in half the common time.
Margin: Nothing in the Reach needs help knitting. Burn it.

LILAC MOON-MOSS. A moss of the drowned stones of Whisper-Grove, which gives a soft lilac light in the jar. I know it only by report from the physicians of the Woods, who prize it above gold for deafness and the ringing of the ears.

Margin: I had a pinch of it off a Woods pedlar the summer before the Grove went quiet, and it still glows in its jar on my sill, which is more than can be said for the pedlar. It is good for ears, the best thing there is. A carter's boy came to me deaf from a powder-flash on the quarry road and it gave him his hearing back in two days, and the first thing he heard was his mother crying at my door, and he did not know what the sound was. Nobody will come up the Grove road selling it again. When my jar is done, it is done.
LIME FLOWER. The blossom of the lime, as grows by every chapel in the province, taken as a tisane for sleep and for a fretful heart.
Margin: The chapel lime here still flowers, and the bees still go to it. Nobody sleeps anyway.
WHITE POPPY. For pain past bearing, given in drops, and at the last, in larger drops, by the physician's own hand and no other's.

Margin: The Grafters have their own drops for this now, the long drops, and they carry them in a brown bottle for the end. I do not know what is in them. I know what they are for, and I am told the surgeon at Oakhaven gives them gently, which is more than I will say for his Office.

On a blank leaf at the back, in her hand: MUTE-DROPS. Yewdale has no page for these, because no physician in his day would have dreamed of them, so I give them one. The Grafting Office's mute-drops: three on the tongue, and a quarter hour. They do not take the pain. They take the voice. A sawboy once left a bottle on my step by mistake. It smelled of bitter almond and wet slate and something I have no name for, and I poured it into the Flume, and the eels came up to look. It is not a herb. It is not physic. They say it is a kindness to the whole street. I say a medicine that is kinder to the street than to the patient is a policy, and I will not have a policy in my book.

Below it: BURL. Neither of us has a page for this. People come to my door asking for a herb for the burl, and there is none. I sold two, the first year, a sorrel wash and a bitter salve, because a woman wept on my step and I could not bear to send her off with nothing. I am ashamed of both. If a child's fingers are putting out white hairs toward the hearth, do not come to me. Keep the hands warm and dry and out of the damp, and go to whoever in your town still sings.

On the inside of the back board: To whoever has this book after me. Yewdale wrote that the physician's whole art in the Reach was to stand aside. Mine has been to stand in the way, mostly of things that wanted to grow. I leave it with the willow page folded down. It is the only page in forty years I never had to correct, and it is bark off a tree, and you peel it on the north side.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part VI (the Reach: law going soft since 417, burl-sick, Grafters) and Part IV (the Narrow); Book One ch. 3 Burl (mute-drops, three on the tongue and a quarter hour; 'They took the voice'; the long drops; sap-mark); Vol I III.1 (Resonant Moss, wounds closing over splinters), Vol II Reach hazard 3 (overgrowth wound) and Greenroot's overgrowth cases; Series Bible Part IV 'The World Went Flat' (milk sours overnight); game items in js/upgrades.js (herb_willow Silver Willow-Bark, herb_reed Sweet Reed-Pith from the Flume banks, herb_moss Lilac Moon-Moss from drowned stone, clears deafening) and js/data.js (Bettany's Tonic: honey, raw egg, willow-bark; rumour 'Nobody has eggs'); Vol VII (b) and Phase 9 text (bees to the chapel lime). Whisper-Grove silenced 416 (Series Bible timeline), so the pedlar's summer is 415. Rooke is referred to only as 'the surgeon at Oakhaven' and only with canon facts. [PROPOSED]: Barnabas Yewdale and his 391 herbal; Prue Gorse, herb-woman, late of Greenroot (moved inside the Hedge at Oakhaven in review, since Greenroot fell silent in 417, js/parish.js and lib_e_undertow_reach); Jem Cutler and his nail; the carter's boy; sweet reed-pith steadying the frightened; the moss sold to the Grafters by the sack; the smell of the mute-drops. Suggested library: the Conservatory in Oakhaven, if not left at Greenroot.

title: Ears After Dark: A Field Guide for Those Who Sit the Crossings
author: Tilda Dunnock, night-hummer of the Tannery Row crossing
summary: An old night-hummer's guide to the sounds of an Oakhaven night, arranged like a bird-book, for the new ones the Watch keeps sending her, who keep standing up.
text: I have sat the Tannery Row crossing every night since the Hedge closed, which is two years and a season, on the same stool and in the same shawl, and the Watch has asked me to write down what I know for the new ones, because the new ones keep standing up. Do not stand up. That is the first thing. A woman standing at a crossing in the dark is a woman about to go somewhere, and everything out there knows it.
This is a guide to listening. I have set it out the way the old bird-books are set out, by what you will hear, and it is short, because most of what you need to know is: hum, and do not answer.

WHAT YOU OUGHT TO HEAR. Learn the town first, so that you know when something is missing from it. A hush-lamp whistles high and thin and never quite steady. There are twenty-two within hearing of my stool, and I know them the way you know your children's coughs. A cradle creaks on the Row at the second hour and again at the fourth. The tavern shutters tick as they cool. The oaks chime when there is wind, and since the quarry, sometimes when there is none. Under all of it, in your teeth more than your ears, the bore. Write your own crossing down, every sound and its hour. You will want the list later.

HOUNDS. You will not hear a hound. You will hear what it has eaten. A hound comes the way rain comes onto a slate roof, a soft quick patter that is not quite in the right place, and inside the patter are sounds that do not belong to the hour: a child laughing where there is no child, a cartwheel where no cart is moving, a man shouting run. Worst and surest of all, a bell. Nobody in the Reach has rung a bell since the Synod took them for the bore, and the hounds still have them. If you hear a bell, it is not a bell.

Before any of that, listen to the roosting birds. A hound goes through a hedgerow like a hot iron through wax, and the birds go still in front of it, one bush at a time. If you hear the quiet walking toward you, it is not quiet. It is something with the birds' silence carried in front of it like a bow-wave.

What draws them: music, first and always, and the louder and the dearer the better. A scream will draw them. A name said aloud draws them faster, and I do not know why, and I would rather not. Keep names indoors after dark.

What to do when you hear one: nothing. Hum lower, not higher, and keep it in your chest. They come to a song, not to a murmur; a murmur is only the town breathing. If one comes close it is not your hum that will save you. It is glass, and you will not have any, so pray the Watch has.

BEDS. In the morning, look for where the dew is not. A hound lies up in an oval a little longer than a big dog, and where it has lain the grass is dry and flat, and no sound carries in it for a day. Drop a pebble in. If you do not hear it land, go round. Birds will not land on a bed. Children will want to stand in one, to see what it is like. Do not let them.

VOICES. This is the part the new ones ask about, and the part I like writing least. You will hear people you love. At the Hedge, mostly, at the dead hour, low and warm and a little tired, the way they sounded at the end of a long day. They will know things. They will know the name you had as a child. They will ask you to come and help them, or they will say that they are cold.

I will put it as plain as I can. Never answer a voice you cannot see. Not to say no. Not to say you are sorry. Answering tells it where you are, and whatever you say, it keeps. A word you give it on Rootday it will give back to you by Nullday, in your own mouth.
A trick works once. If you and your sister have a whistle that means come home, and you use it where it can be heard, it is its whistle now. Make another, and do not use that one either.

I know a man who listens to his wife at a crossing. Everybody knows him. I will not name him, because none of us has the heart. He does not answer. He only listens. I put him in so that you will understand I am not telling you what is easy.
SILENCE. Silence comes in three kinds, and you must learn the first two by heart, so that you are never mistaken about the third.

The first is the Hedge's silence. Wool and thorn swallow sound. Stand near the Hedge and your own voice comes back to you small and close, as if you were talking into a pillow. That is a good silence. That is a silence somebody made, on purpose and by hand, for you.
The second is the silence a hound leaves. It is dry, like the bed. It sits in one place, it does not move, and it wears off by the next night.

The third I will not write about. My mother said a thing written down is a thing invited, and I have sat out too many nights to start sending invitations now. I will tell you only how you will know. You will notice that you cannot hear something you ought to: the reed in the lamp, the cradle at the second hour, your own breath. And it will not frighten you. That is how you will know. When you notice it, hum. Hum anything, and hum it badly. Say your own name into your shawl.

WHAT WE FIND IN THE MORNING. Once in my two years I went to relieve a crossing at the far end of the town at first light, and I found the stool, and the shawl folded on it, and the lamp still burning, and the reed in the lamp gone still. Nobody on that street had heard a thing. That is the whole of the entry. I have put it here so that you will not stand up.

That is all I know. Sit down. Keep the shawl on. Hum. When the shift changes at the dead hour, say it to the one who comes to take your stool: all's well, all's quiet, keep to the Narrow. Say it when it is not true. It is not for them. It is so that there is a voice at the crossing.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part IV (the Narrow; night-hummers at crossings; the mimic rule, 'Never answer a voice you cannot see'; a trick works on a mimic once; hounds come to music; a hound's bed where no sound carries for a day); Book One ch. 1 (Listening Hour, the shift change 'all's well, all's quiet, keep to the Narrow', hush-lamps' thin reed-whistle, the bore in her teeth, no bells since the Synod took them for bore-teeth), ch. 2 (the bed: no dew, a pebble makes no sound, no bird will land), ch. 4 (the hounds' stolen sounds: a baby laughing, a cartwheel, a bell, a man screaming run), ch. 6 (the jitter 'like rain beginning on a slate roof'; the shared whistle learned by the Wearer). Tam listening to his dead wife at the Flume crossing (js/data.js rumour) appears unnamed. Vol II bestiary 'a spoken name draws more than a scream'. The Hush is never described: only absence (the lamp's reed gone still, the folded shawl), following Vol IV 1.8 rule 4 ('you cannot hear something you should') and rule 2 (it does not frighten). [PROPOSED]: Tilda Dunnock and her two years at the Tannery Row crossing; the Watch asking for a written guide; twenty-two lamps in hearing; the birds going still before a hound; the three silences; the empty stool at the far crossing. title: The Fellers' Book: On the Cutting of Iron-Bough
author: Jethro Nettleford, feller-master of Oakhaven; with a postscript by Tomas, timber-cutter
summary: A gruff old feller-master's lessons for apprentices on knocking, felling and naming the timber that rings like bronze, and what his last apprentice had to add after the Hedge went up.
text: Iron-bough is not timber. Get that into your head on your first day and you will keep your fingers longer than I kept mine. Timber is dead wood. Iron-bough is a tree that has not yet agreed to be dead, and the whole of the fellers' craft is the getting of that agreement.

I have felled in the Reach for forty-one years and trained eleven apprentices. Nine are living. Two have beams named after them in the Greenhall roof, which is the only memorial a feller gets, and which neither of them would have chosen, being careless men.

ON KNOWING THE GROVE. A grove knows its own. Walk into a stand of iron-bough as a stranger and the trees go quiet round you, a ring of quiet that widens as you walk, and every feller in the valley lifts his head and says: somebody is in the north stand who oughtn't to be. So you do not cut a grove you have not walked. An apprentice walks his master's grove every evening for a month before he is let near it with an edge, until the trees chime round him as they chime round anyone else. Then he is furniture to them, and he may begin.

ON THE KNOCK. Before you cut, you knock. Strike the trunk with the back of your axe at shoulder height, and listen. A sound tree gives you a clean bronze note that hangs in the air as long as a held breath. A buzz in it means worm. Two notes at once means the heart is split, and the tree will twist as it goes. A dead note, a knock like a fist on a door with nobody home, means hollow, and you leave it, because a hollow iron-bough falls where it likes. Chalk the note on the bark. Your master will check it. He will be right and you will be wrong for about four years.

ON THE SINGING DOWN. No feller in the Reach puts an edge to an old tree until a Cantor has sung it down. This is not piety. I have no piety. It is practical. The felling-song tells the sap to go down and the tree to sleep, and a sleeping tree falls true, splits clean, and does not throw its crown back at you. I have seen a tree felled awake. It took Jago Holcombe's arm off at the shoulder and then lay there ringing for an hour as if it were pleased with itself. Wait for the Cantor. Pay her in cider. Stand still while she sings and take your hat off, and if you laugh I will put you in the Flume.

ON THE FELL. Cut the mouth on the side you want her to fall, a third of the way through, then the back-cut a hand higher. Do not cut through the hinge; the hinge steers her. When she begins to go, step back along the line you have already cleared, and never run, because a man running cannot hear what the tree is doing.

ON RINGING-WOOD DAY. We fell for the year at the first hard frost, when the sap is lowest, and the whole of Oakhaven comes out to hear it. Each trunk rings as it falls, and a big one rings for as long as it takes to sing the Sheaf Song through, and the children run under the note as if it were rain. Then the beams are named. Every beam in a Reach house has a name, cut small on the end-grain where it sits in the wall: the name of the tree, or of the feller, or of somebody's grandmother, or a joke. The beam over my own bed is called Not Tonight. My wife named it.

ON THE WOOD AFTER. Iron-bough goes on growing a little after it is cut, a hair a year, which is why Reach doors stick in the spring and why you must never trust a joiner from outside the province. A good beam rings faintly for years whenever the house is struck. Your grandchildren will know the beams you cut by their notes. That is all the fame a feller ever gets, and it is better than most.
Mind your hands. Mind your master. Wait for the Cantor. J. Nettleford, Feller-Master, Oakhaven, the back-end of 406.
POSTSCRIPT, in a different hand, written larger. Jethro is dead seven years and cannot argue, so here is what has changed. I am Tomas. I was his twelfth and his last; he had me one winter.

Everything he says about the knock is still true, and the knock will now get you killed. The wood rings louder since the quarry, and a bell-note in the open brings hounds the way a supper-bell brings boys. So: carded wool on the blade, bound tight, four strokes to a bundle before it beats flat. Cut in a gust, when the whole grove is chiming anyway and one more note is lost in it. If a hound comes up, stop. Call the job off. Leave the tree a day to forget the hour you were at it. Never run with a log. A log knocks against everything you own.

There is no Cantor to sing them down now. The orchard-cantor was taken the year of the Hedge, and you do not ask a Cantor to sing above the Narrow for a tree when she has a whole town to sing small for. So we lay a palm flat on the bark and say sorry, quietly, and I do not know if it helps. They fall awake. They throw their crowns and kick the saw. I have lost three fingers to it, and the fourth grew back wrong, and I keep it in a glove, and I will not show it you.

We held Ringing-Wood Day last back-end in the lee of the Hedge, with wool on every blade. Nobody came out to hear. Nobody named a beam. The timber goes up the quarry road on the Synod's quota to shore a headframe, and a headframe does not want a name.

Jethro wrote that your grandchildren will know your beams by their notes. Mine are holding up a hole in the ground. I have thought what I like of myself since Firstfruit. Knock first anyway. It is the only honest thing left in the job.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part VI (the oaks ring like bronze; the quarry; bells taken); Vol II Reach (Tomas, timber-cutter, three fingers missing, the fourth grew back wrong and kept in a glove; hazard 6 ringing timber draws hounds; the silent circle round a stranger, also Vol I III.1); Vol I 6.5 (iron-bough rings like bronze and grows); Vol V 4 (the felling-song, sung to an old tree before the axe, tells the sap to go down and the tree to sleep); Vol VII (b) 2 (Ringing-Wood Day at the first hard frost, trunks ring as they fall, beams named; the Sheaf Song); Phase 9 quest 'Tomas's Last Load' (wool from the mill on the blade, four strokes a bundle, a gust, leave the wood a day to forget the hour, do not run with the log, Synod quota, timber shores the Consortium headframe); Tobin taken 417 (Series Bible). Book is set before 18 Frostmonth 419, when wood stopped ringing (Vol V). title: The Narrow Larder: Receipts for a Lean Year, with Remarks
author: Philippa Oatley, who kept the cookshop by the market, Oakhaven
summary: An Oakhaven cook's receipts from the Fracture winter and the shut years since, for bread that will not stop rising, pies with no egg, and suppers nobody else needs to hear.
text: Hetty says I am to write it down before I die, so that somebody in this town can still make a pie that does not go off like a mortar. I said I would, if she put it on her shelf where people could see it and not under the bar with the strong cider. She has promised. If you are reading this under the bar, take it out.

THE FIRST LEAN YEAR. Everybody under twenty thinks the lean years began with the Hedge. They did not. They began on the morning the sky rang, in 412, and the winter after was the worst eating this valley has had in anyone's memory. Milk turned between the pail and the dairy door. Cheese would not take. The cider went flat in the barrel, a quarter-tone flat, and the old men said they could taste it, and they could. The harvest went into the barns heavy and came out of them grey and tasting of nothing. Then the wagons came up the Greenroot road with grain, and the Governor said we would eat, and we ate, and nobody in this house asked what it cost. I will not start asking in a cookery book.
RECEIPTS OF THE FRACTURE WINTER, for when it comes again.

Hedge pottage. Nettles, cut young and with gloves; sorrel; a handful of barley if you have it, and an onion if you are a Governor. Boil. Do not salt it, because there is no salt. There will be salt later, and you will weep over it.

Acorn cake. Iron-bough acorns, which nobody ate before 412 and everybody ate after. Shell them and leach them in the Flume in a net for three days, or they will turn your mouth inside out. Pound them in a mortar. They ring in the mortar, so put a cloth over it. Bake flat on a hot stone. It tastes of a floor, but a clean floor.

Eel boiled twice. The Flume eel is green, and so is its broth, and the first water is not for drinking. Pour it off, fresh water, and boil again. Wrap what is left in dock-leaf. Children will not eat it the first time. They will eat it the third.
WHAT WE EAT NOW.

Bread. Since the quarry, bread wants to rise and does not know when to stop. Punch it down. Punch it down again. Never leave dough to prove overnight. I have seen a loaf come up out of its crock and across a table like a sleeping cat, and the woman next door had to take her oven door off with a crowbar. Bake in a lidded crock with a stone on the lid, and listen. Good bread is quiet. Bread that creaks is not done growing.

Flour. The fields regrow overnight now, which sounds like a mercy until you taste the third cutting. First-cut flour is for bread, second for porridge, and the third for the paste you hang wallpaper with. Keep the Last Sheaf's flour for the hearth bread and nothing else. The last stand is still uncut in the north field as I write this, so you know the time of year, and they are saying the Church will want it put off. We shall see.

Mutton. There is none. The flocks went into the Hedge for their wool, and then they went into us, one a month, and I cooked a good many of them myself, and I am not sorry. If anyone in this town sells you mutton pie, ask him whose. If he says it is lamb, ask him whose lamb.

Eggs. There are none. The hens went quiet first, the autumn after the Hedge went in. I will not say more than that, and what was left of them went in the pot. To bind a pie without egg: a spoon of honey and a spoon of flour, beaten with a little cider. To glaze it: milk, if you can get milk that has not turned, which you cannot, so do not glaze it. Nobody in Oakhaven has looked at a shiny pie in two years and we are none the worse for it.

Bettany's tonic, which she gives for weakness, is honey, raw egg and willow-bark. When you ask her where the egg comes from she looks at you as if you had asked her where babies come from, and she of all women should know.

Moot-curd. Aged beside a humming stone, and it tastes faintly of static, the way the air does before thunder. It is the one thing in this book that has got better since 412. I do not know why and I have stopped asking it.

COOKING QUIET. Felt your lids. Wooden spoons, and never iron on iron. Take the kettle off before it sings; a kettle that sings is a kettle calling. Grind before dusk. Chop on a folded cloth. If you must crack a bone for the marrow, do it under water in a bucket. Nobody needs to hear your supper but you.

THE LAST RECEIPT, FOR THE SHEAF. When the last field is cut, every house in the Reach bakes hearth bread from the new flour, one round loaf, and it is broken by hand and never cut, and you give the first piece to whoever is oldest at the table, and the heel to the youngest, and the crumbs to the hearth. That is the whole receipt. You do not need me for it. Your grandmother did it, and so will you.

If the Church will not let us keep the Sheaf this year, bake the bread anyway, after dark, and break it with the shutters to and the lamp low, and pass it round, and eat it. That is all lean-year cookery has ever been. You eat anyway, and you eat together, and you eat quietly. The rest is only salt.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part IV (World Went Flat: milk sours overnight; the Narrow) and Part VI (law going soft since 417; bread that rises until the oven splits, Part IV law-rot); Governor Aldric fed the town in the Cascade famine (Series Bible VIII), told here only as wagons up the Greenroot road and an unasked price; Vol I III.1 (cider, hearth bread, river eel, moot-curd aged beside a humming stone tasting faintly of static; grain regrowing within a day and tasting of less); Vol VII (b) (the Last Sheaf hung on the Hedge-gate, hearth bread from the new flour; the Church postponed it in 419); Phase 20-21 Author Rulings (the flocks went into the Hedge's wool and were eaten in the two shut years); js/data.js (Bettany's Tonic: honey, raw egg, willow-bark; rumour 'Nobody has eggs. The hens went quiet first.'); js/upgrades.js (Smoked Flume-Eel boiled twice); market lines in js/calendar11.js (eel in dock-leaf). Hetty Bram of the Boar & Dulcimer is mentioned only as keeping a shelf. [PROPOSED]: Philippa Oatley and her cookshop; acorn cake from iron-bough acorns; the three cuttings of flour; binding a pie with honey and flour; the hearth-bread custom of first piece to the eldest. Suggested library: the Boar & Dulcimer, or sold at the market.

title: Telling the Bees
author: Ennis Crowle, beekeeper, of the Flume road
summary: A beekeeper of the Flume road writes down, for the first time in her family's memory, how to keep straw skeps in the Narrow and how to tell the bees the news.
text: My mother kept bees on the Flume road, and her mother before her, and none of us ever wrote anything down, because a bee-woman's craft goes from mouth to ear, close, at the straw, the way everything that matters goes. But there are fewer mouths every year, and fewer ears, and the young ones who come to me for a swarm do not know how to tell. So I have written it in the plainest words I have, and if the bees think the less of me for it, they may say so.

SKEPS. Coil the straw and bind it with split bramble, never twine. Set the skep on a stone stool in the lee of a wall, with a straw hackle over it for the rain. A good hive hums low and steady, like a kettle thinking about it. Learn your own hive's hum the first week, because everything is in it. A hive that has lost its queen howls: a thin, ragged, high note that you will hear from the road, and that makes the dogs uneasy.

Since the quarry, the bees work too fast. Comb draws itself out overnight. I have had a skep fill in a week that ought to have taken a summer, and brood come out of season in the back-end. Take the honey early and often, or the comb will grow through the straw and split the skep from the inside.

TELLING. The bees must be told. Every birth and every death in the household, and every stranger who comes to stay. If they are not told, they go. You come out one morning and the straw is empty and still warm, and they are off in the wood, hanging in a clump on a branch like a bruise, waiting for somebody who will tell them things. My grandmother said the bees are the house's ears. I think it is simpler than that. They live with us, and they want to know what we know. So would you.

How to tell. Go at dusk, when they are all home. Stand close, closer than is comfortable, with your mouth near the straw. Knock once, softly, two knuckles and one tap, the way we knock in Oakhaven. Then murmur the news. Not loud. A bee minds a shout worse than a hound does. Say it plainly. A girl born to the house, and her name. Or the name of who has died, and that they are gone and will not be coming to the hives again. If there is more than one dead, tell them in the order of the years, oldest first, so the bees can keep them straight. Tell a stranger by name, and where they came from, and that they are to be let past. Then wait. When the hive has had it, the hum settles lower, the way a room changes when somebody has made room on the bench.

In my mother's day you sang it. There was a telling-song, four lines, which I will not write here, because nobody may sing it now, and a song written down and never sung is a sad thing to leave lying on a page.

SINCE THE HEDGE. When they planted the Hedge, they took every fleece in the Reach for the wool, and I gave my skeps' winter wrappings with the rest. That first winter a hive's hum carried a quarter mile on a still night, and the hounds came down the Flume road to it twice. I lost two skeps, and very nearly my own self. So now I wrap them in fleece again, bought dear, and I set them in the lee of the reed-banks where the water talks over them.
A hum is a sound, and a sound brings hounds, and there is no help for that. But a hive that has not been told goes, and a hive that goes leaves you with nothing at all, and I would rather the hum.

HONEY. Reach honey is the Cantors' honey. Warmed in the hand and stirred with a drop of oil, it is what they take for a torn throat, and every Cantor in the Reach has a torn throat now. I give it free to any Cantor who comes up the road. So should you.

MY OWN TELLING. When I die, somebody go down the Flume road and tell them. Go at dusk. Knock once. Tell them Ennis has gone and will not be coming to the hives again, and that they are to stay for whoever comes next. They will know already; bees always know. Tell them anyway. It was never for them that we did it.
notes: Canon: Book Four Part One and Vol V 4 (Ennis Crowle, who kept bees on the Flume road; nothing else about her is used, and her later fate is not mentioned); Phase 9 quest 'Telling the Bees' (straw skeps bound with bramble; in the Reach you tell the bees every birth and death or they go; the three tellings: a birth, the dead in order of the years, the stranger; murmur close at the straw; bees hang in clumps 'like a bruise'; the hive hums 'like a kettle thinking about it'; 'Bees mind a shout worse than hounds do'; a hum draws hounds, fleece for the skeps; bees to the orchard and chapel lime); Phase 20-21 Rulings and Book Four (every fleece in the Reach went into the Hedge in 417); Series Bible Part VI (law going soft since 417); js/data.js (Oiled Honey for the throat); Book One ch. 3 (the soft Oakhaven knock, two knuckles, one tap). [PROPOSED]: that Ennis wrote this book; her mother and grandmother as bee-women; the queenless howl; comb drawn overnight since the quarry; the lost telling-song; skeps set in the lee of the reed-banks; free honey for Cantors. Suggested library: the Conservatory in Oakhaven, or Lyra's lending shelf.

title: Reed and Lamp: On Cutting Flume-Reed and Making Hush-Lamp Whistles
author: Dorran Sedge, keeper of the river gate, Oakhaven
summary: The river-gate keeper who once tended the Cantors' reed-beds explains, at length and against his wife's wishes, how to cut Flume-reed, why a cut reed dies in a day, and how a hush-lamp whistles.
text: I kept the reed-beds at Reedside for the Conservatory before I kept the river gate, which is near thirty years with my hands in reed one way and another, and Mabbie says that if I am going to talk about it every supper I may as well write it down and talk about something else at supper. So.

First, what is gone. The orchard wind-reed is gone. For three hundred years the Cantors planted it in rows and pruned it to pitch, until a whole valley of it would sing a chord when the wind came off the hills, and I tended those rows from a boy. On the morning the sky rang, every wind-reed in the Reach went to something like spun sugar in an hour, and the next wind took it. I was at the river gate that morning. I heard the orchards stop. I will not write more than that.

What is left is Flume-reed, the wild cousin, that grows in the wet along the channel, under the river gate and down past the lower lock. It was never planted, never pruned, and never taught a note in its life, and my belief, which the Conservatory has never asked for, is that this is why it lived. The orchard reed had been told what to be for three hundred years. When the world went a quarter-tone wrong it had nothing of its own to fall back on. Flume-reed had never been told anything. It just went on being reed.

CUTTING. Cut at dusk, when the reed has been drinking all day. Cut low and on the slant, one clean stroke, with a knife you keep for nothing else, and lay the reed in wet moss at once. Three from a bed in a day and no more, or the bed sulks and gives you nothing for a week. Cut quietly. A reed-knife makes no sound if you know your business, and if you do not know your business the hounds will teach it you.

WHY A CUT REED DIES IN A DAY. Every cutter is asked this and every cutter has his own answer. Mine is that a cut reed is a reed waiting to be told what it is. While it is green it will hold any pitch you give it. Give it one before this time tomorrow and it will keep that note the year round, till the next Reed-Hanging, and longer if you oil it. Leave it untold past the day and it gives up waiting. It goes pale and light and brittle, and it will not take a note again for love or money. A dry reed is good for kindling and nothing else. Do not keep dry reeds about the house. Mabbie says they look like bad news, and she is right.

TUNING. You tune by the slot and by the length. Cut the lip with a fine knife, a sliver at a time, blowing across it between cuts, until the note sits where you want it. A reed is tuned against the Root note, a hundred and seventy-four, which any Cantor will give you and most old men can hum. For a First Reed you want the child's own note, and the Cantor finds that for you; I have cut the reeds for half the children on the river street. For a lamp you want nobody's note at all.

THE HUSH-LAMP. A hush-lamp is a lamp with a reed in its chimney. The heat goes up, the draught draws across the reed's lip, and the reed speaks for as long as the flame burns: high and thin and never quite steady. The unsteadiness is the whole of the art. A steady note is a thing that can be learned and followed. A wavering one is only the house breathing.

To make one, you want a brass collar to hold the reed above the throat of the chimney, a hand's width over the flame and no closer, or it scorches. Set the slot to face the draught. Seal the collar with beeswax; Ennis Crowle's, from the Flume road, is the best, and she will tell you so herself. Tune a lamp-reed a little sharp of the Root, and never to any living person's note. A lamp that sounds like a person is a lamp that something may come and talk to.

Trim your wick right. Too high and the reed shrieks. Too low and it stops, and a lamp that is burning with its reed stopped is worse than a dark one, because you will look at the flame and think you are safe. Listen to your lamp before you sleep. If you cannot hear it, get up.

OIL AND FROST. Oil your reeds once a month, colza or a drop of lamp-oil on a rag. A reed cracks in the dry and splits in the frost, and a First Reed that splits is a grief to a house. If it splits, the note is not lost. Any old body who knew the person can hum it near enough, and a reed tuned near enough is still a comfort. A reed that is a little wrong is a comfort, sometimes, in a way that a right one is not.

REED-HANGING. In Reedmonth, when the reed comes up, every house takes down last year's reeds and hangs new ones, tuned to each child in it. The street used to be loud with tuning for a day; you could not hear yourself think on the river street for the whistling. These last two years we have done it with our mouths an inch from the reed and the doors shut, and you would not know from the street that anything had happened at all. Every door on the river street has a new reed over it all the same.

People ask me why I bother, when nobody past the thorn will hear a reed of ours again, with the Hedge eating every note before it is halfway down the lane. I tell them a reed does not have to be heard to be right. It only has to be given its note.
Mabbie says that is enough about reed. It is never enough about reed. D. Sedge, at the river gate.
notes: Canon: Vol V 4 and js/prologue17.js (Dorran Sedge kept the river gate for twenty years and the reed-beds at Reedside before that; his wife Mabbie; nothing of his later story is used); Book One ch. 1 (the orchard wind-reeds turned to spun sugar on the day the Spire broke and blew away; hush-lamp reed-whistle; First Reeds; Tobin's reed-pipes oiled monthly because they crack in the dry); Phase 20-21 Rulings review note (game reeds are to be called Flume-reeds, since wind-reed died in 412); Vol I 6.5 (wind-reed holds any pitch and dies in a day) and 4.3 (the First Reed); js/reedcraft.js (reed beds by the Flume crossing, three a bed a day, a cut reed lives one day then turns to a dry reed that will burn; tuned against 174; First Reed tuned to a person); Phase 9 quest 'A Reed for Pellow' (a split reed retuned to a hummed note; 'a comfort to have it wrong'); Vol VII (b) (Reed-Hanging in Reedmonth); js/data.js oil item (colza oil). [PROPOSED]: Dorran writing this book; his theory that Flume-reed lived because it was never taught; why a cut reed dies (it is waiting to be told); hush-lamp construction (brass collar, a hand's width above the flame, beeswax seal, lamp-reed tuned a little sharp of the Root and never to a person); the wick rule; Reed-Hanging done mouth-to-reed behind shut doors. Suggested library: the Bonded Store at Stillwater Landing (lamp-reeds are a Flume trade), or the Conservatory.

title: Tank and Envelope: A Handbook for the Riggers and Tank-Tuners of Envelope Ships
author: Ondine Abara, yard-mistress of the drift-yard below the Long Mole, Port Cantabile; this copy with pencil notes signed P.
year: 410 SR (fourth printing, 415 SR); pencil notes 417–419 SR
summary: A Rust Coast yard-mistress's sharp-tongued handbook on persuading drift-glass to lift and keeping an old envelope ship in the air, in a copy a young engineer has argued with in pencil.
text: This book is for the rigger and the tank-tuner of an envelope ship: sixty feet or thereabouts, oak and brass, a sailcloth envelope over her, lift-tanks slung beneath her keel. It is not for the courier-cutters, which have no envelope and no manners, nor for the great Consortium freighters, whose engineers will not read a book written by a woman who learned her trade on a slipway. You know who you are. Your ship is older than you, and patched like a quilt, and you love her more than is sensible.

ON DRIFT-GLASS. Everything begins with the glass. Drift-glass is Velocity glass tuned to lift. It is pale green as sea-ice when you hold it in your hand, and packed in a brass tank with a reed-valve at one end it burns a soft cobalt and wants, above all things, to move. The whole art of the envelope ship lies in persuading it that the way it most wants to move is up. Her core is another matter: Fortis-cut lodestone in an iron cage amidships, which takes the weight off her and asks nothing of you. Leave it to the Fortis men. The core makes her light. The glass makes her go. You do not command drift-glass. You persuade it. Captains do not understand this, and it is no use telling them.

ON LISTENING TO A TANK. A tank is full of song. When she is content she hums a low chord that you feel through the deck in your heels. Learn that chord in your first week aboard, as you would learn your mother's voice, because everything you need to know is in it. A sour note in the chord means the glass is unsettled: damp in the valve, a knock in the cradle, or salt. Salt above all. Salt gets into a tank and makes her moody, and a moody tank lifts in sulks and starts, and you will spend your nights with a tuning-hammer putting her right.
Pencil, in the margin: She likes to be told what you are going to do before you do it. Not in the book. True, though. P.
ON THE TUNING-HAMMER. Felt head, brass shaft, never iron. Tap the cradle, never the tank. A tap on the tank itself is an insult, and she will remember it for a week.
Pencil: Mine. Not the captain's. He uses it on the galley stove. P.

ON THE ENVELOPE. The envelope keeps what the tanks breathe out, gives her the last of her lift, and gives her most of her temper in a wind. Close-woven sailcloth, doped every season. Patch inside and outside both, in long laps, and stitch with the grain. A patch is no disgrace. An unpatched hole is.
Pencil: Better than sailcloth for a weep: weaverling silk. Do not ask where it came from. Deep Woods, 419. P.

ON BALLAST. Iron in the keel-sling. It is what keeps her from flying like a leaf in a squall. Every new captain wants to throw it over to make height, and every old rigger has watched what happens next.

ON LIFT. Do your figures on a slate, and do them twice, and when the captain does not like the answer, do them a third time and give him the same answer. A soul is a hundredweight and a half with his boots on, a child half that, and in the whole history of skyships nobody has ever come aboard with less baggage than he said he had. Water is the heaviest thing you carry that you cannot do without. The long gun is the heaviest thing you carry that you can.
Pencil: Eighteen. Not twenty. I said so. P.

ON A WEEPING TANK. Drift-glass does not burst. If a tank is holed, it weeps: a slow cobalt vapour, and the lift goes out with it. You will hear it before you see it, because the chord goes thin and climbs. Clip the hole, seal the clip, and get her down while you still choose where. A clipped tank is good for forty miles if you are lucky and four if you are not. A whole new tank wants a drift-bench and a yard, and somebody who knows how to tune one. There is a yard below the Long Mole, and I am somebody.
Pencil: Forty miles, then Cantabile. He will not like it. P.

ADDED TO THE FOURTH PRINTING: ON FLYING IN THE NARROW. Since the Screaming Year, riggers have asked me what the hounds make of a ship. At height, nothing on the ground hears her. Below a hundred feet a sour tank carries further than you would credit, and a hound will follow a chord as it follows a song. Keep her sweet when you are low. Moor high. Do not shout orders over the rail; learn hand-cant, as the deaf bosuns do, and hire one if you can. And if at the dead hour you hear your mother calling you from the rigging, it is not your mother, and you are not to go up.

ON THE WINCH AND THE LINE. A winch drum is only as strong as the deck-beams it is bolted through, and the beams are only as strong as the hull they hold together. If whatever hangs on the end of your line is heavier than your ship can lift, it is your ship that will go down to it, not the other way about. Keep an axe beside every drum. Everybody on the Coast knows the saying: the line is not a promise; the line is a rope.
There is no pencil note here. Somebody has underlined the last sentence, once, very hard, so that the lead has gone through the paper.

A LAST WORD. A ship is not a house. She is a set of arguments with the air that you win every day by a little, and lose all at once if you stop making them. Riggers come and go. Ships, if you are good at your work, stay. Be good at your work.
Pencil, on the back board, smaller than the rest: She hums sweeter when I sleep on the tanks. Mags says that is only my snoring. Mags cannot hear my snoring. P.
notes: Canon: Book One ch. 4 (the Drift-Kestrel: sixty feet of brass rib and oak plank under a grey sailcloth envelope patched like a quilt; lift-tanks below her keel glowing the cobalt of drift-glass; 'Drift-glass wanted, above all things, to move'; persuading it that up is the way; a contented chord, a sour note; Pennick asleep on the tanks with his tuning-hammer; 'Salt gets in her tanks and makes her moody'; Mags deaf, hand-cant, Free Captains paying double for deaf bosuns), ch. 8 (lift figures on a slate, done three times; iron ballast in the keel-sling; the long gun; eighteen, maybe nineteen, not twenty), ch. 12 epigraph ('The line is not a promise. The line is a rope.', Rust Coast saying; the winch drum bolted through the deck-beams), ch. 21 (Office courier-cutter with no envelope, four hard drift-tanks; drift-glass weeps a cobalt vapour), ch. 24 (a clipped tank good for perhaps forty miles; a whole tank needs a yard with a drift-bench; Port Cantabile); Book Two Part One ch. 4 (drift-glass is Velocity glass tuned to lift, pale green as sea-ice, packed in brass with a reed-valve; 'A tank is full of song'); js/data.js item liftsilk and js/kestrel16.js (a tank closed with weaverling silk). Vol IV Rust Coast (the Long Mole). The Screaming Year is 412 (Series Bible). P. is Pennick only by implication; the notes use only what canon gives him (he talks to and sleeps on the tanks, does the lift figures, argues with Vane). [PROPOSED]: Ondine Abara and her drift-yard below the Long Mole; the book and its 415 chapter; tapping the cradle not the tank; hounds following a sour tank below a hundred feet; a soul at a hundredweight and a half; the hard underlining. Suggested library: the Kestrel below decks, or the Bonded Store at Stillwater Landing (a smugglers' book room would stock a Cantabile rigging manual). Owner ruling (Oct 2026): a volume stands. Vol I §§ Fortis, Skyships: every skyship has a Fortis-cut lodestone core that cancels mass; the manuscript's drift-glass lift-tanks give the lift.

title: Handbook of the Grafting Office (Oakhaven Works Issue)
author: The Grafting Office of the Iron Synod; this copy annotated in ink in an unknown hand
origin: the Organum; issued at the Oakhaven Works
summary: The Synod's regulations for surgeons who cut the burl-sick, in the Office's flat hand, with a working surgeon's replies in the margin.
text: HANDBOOK OF THE GRAFTING OFFICE. Issued under the authority of the Office for the use of Surgeon-Grafters and their attendants in provinces subject to law-rot. Oakhaven Works Issue, 417 SR. This handbook is the property of the Office. It is not to be lent, copied or annotated.
Margin, in small neat ink: Annotated.

1. Of the Grafter. The Surgeon-Grafter is an officer of the Synod and not of the household. He attends the patient on behalf of the street. His first duty is to the silence of the street, his second to the law of the province, and his third to the patient.
Margin: Read it backwards.

2. Of attendance. Inspections are made every second Rootday. The Grafter is accompanied by two attendants, styled sawboys, by a brazier of banked coals in an iron cage, and by an escort. Harness is to be felted and hooves booted. The Grafter will wear the mask, which renders the breath at the level of the Narrow, at all times in the patient's house.
Margin: Not for the children. They have enough to look at.

3. Of examination. The affected part is to be examined by lens and by pressure, and the sound of the pressure attended to. Living tissue gives. Tissue gone to wood answers. The chest is to be examined by trumpet below the collarbone for the dry sound, which signifies roots in the lung and places the patient beyond the remedy of the saw.
Margin: It sounds like wind in barley. You will not forget it the first time, so do not try.

4. Of the mute-drops. The patient must not be permitted to cry out. Administer the mute-drops a quarter hour before the first incision, and remind the family that silence is a mercy extended to the whole street. The drops do not relieve pain, and the Grafter is not to represent to the family that they do.
Margin: Somebody must hold the head. The Office does not say who. In this town the Cantor is usually there before you. Let her.

5. Of the instruments. The hush-saw, felted at the grip, with a blade thin enough to flex. The sap-iron, heated at the brazier and applied to the cut surface to stop the bleed, which in this province is green and slow to cease. No instrument is to be laid on stone or permitted to fall.
Margin: The sap-iron is the one loud thing in the morning. Warn them before it, not after.

6. Of the sap-mark. Where the patient is found past remedy by the saw, the Grafter will chalk the outer door in green: a circle, with one line struck through. The mark signifies past cutting. The household so marked is to be visited monthly and kept comfortable, and at the last the long drops are to be administered by the Grafter's own hand.
Margin: That is all it means. Write it on the door small, and tell them what it means before you go, so that they do not have to ask the street.

7. Of the register. The Grafter keeps a register of marked households, giving the name, the house and the date of marking. The register is the property of the Synod. It is to be surrendered without delay to any officer of the Church or of the Arbiterium presenting a warrant under seal.
Something was written in the margin here and scraped away with a knife, more than once, until the paper is thin enough to see the lamp through.
8. Of children. Children are to be inspected as adults are. Early signs in the hands are to be recorded, and are not to be left to the judgement of the family.
Margin: Unusual is also a word. So is recheck next month.

9. Of conduct. The Grafter will not hum, sing, pray aloud or converse with the patient beyond the questions required. The Grafter will not express to the family any opinion as to the justice of the procedure.
Margin: No. But I may go slowly. Nothing here says how fast.
10. Of this Handbook. The Grafter will keep this Handbook about his person and consult it in all cases of doubt.
Margin: I do. In every case. And then I consult the margin.
notes: Canon: Book One ch. 3 Burl, epigraph quoted verbatim as article 4 ('The patient must not be permitted to cry out. Administer the mute-drops a quarter hour before the first incision, and remind the family that silence is a mercy extended to the whole street.' Handbook of the Grafting Office, Oakhaven Works); the same chapter for every detail of practice: Grafters every second Rootday, felted harness and leather-booted hooves, brazier of banked coals in an iron cage, sawboys, a Carillon escort, white masks with a wire lattice so breath comes through in the Narrow, Rooke unmasking for children, brass lens and pressing, the trumpet below the collarbone and the dry rustle like wind in barley, mute-drops take the voice not the pain, hush-saw with felted grip and flexing blade, the sap-iron the only loud sound, the green circle with a line struck through meaning past cutting, monthly visits and the long drops, the Inquisitor demanding the list; Pim's case ('Unusual... Recheck next month'); 'She went ahead of him. He went slowly.' Series Bible VIII (Rooke; sap-mark now also the Inquisitor's list) and js/data.js topic 'The Grafters'. The annotator is not named; readers may infer Rooke, and the notes only echo his canon conduct. [PROPOSED]: the handbook's numbered articles beyond the canon epigraph, the 417 Oakhaven Works issue, green bleed 'slow to cease', the register's form, and the scraped-out note. Suggested library: Rooke's surgery; a stolen copy would also suit the Bonded Store at Stillwater Landing.

title: Rudd's Back-End Book: Signs of Weather for the Downs and the Reach
author: Absalom Rudd, beacon-keeper of the sheep-walk
summary: The old keeper of the fold-fires sets down the weather-signs his father taught him, marks which of them have lied since the sky rang, and admits to one he has no sign for.
text: I kept the fold-fires on three hills for forty back-ends, and a beacon-keeper who cannot read weather is only a man setting fire to good furze. These are the signs I go by. My father gave me most of them and his father gave him the rest. Since the sky rang, about half of them lie. I have marked those, so that you know which half.

A clerk will tell you it is Harvestmonth. A shepherd will tell you the sorrel has gone red and the swallows are lined up on the barn ridge. Down here a month is what is growing, and I have set the signs out that way. If you want the clerk's name for it, ask a clerk.
WHEN THE REED SPEARS.
When the Flume-reed shows its first green spear, the frosts are done. Still true.
A ring round the moon, rain inside three days. Still true. The moon does not care what anybody drilled.
Cows lying down before noon, rain by evening. I cannot tell you. I have not seen a cow on this side of the Downs since the Hedge.
WHEN THE HAY IS DOWN.

Red sky at night, a fair morning. Half a lie. The reds are not as red as they were; everybody over thirty will tell you so, and the young ones think we are mad. Judge by the gold in it instead. Gold still means fair.
A dog howling at noon means a death in the house. A lie. Since 412 every dog in the Octave howls at noon. Feed him and pay him no heed.
Milk turning in the pail means thunder coming. A lie. Since 412 milk turns overnight whatever the sky does.

When the oaks in the valley ring in a still air, there is wind behind the hill. That was true. Since the quarry they ring when they please. I no longer know what they are telling me, and I do not like to guess.
WHEN THE SORREL REDDENS, which is the back-end, and my season.

A heavy year for rowan, a hard winter. True, so far as a Reach winter is ever hard, which is not very. The valley never gets more than a skin of frost, bar the one winter after the sky rang, which I do not count; the Downs get a white morning or two, and the old men stamp and call it weather. My father said the Reach was kept warm from underneath. I have never had a better explanation, and I have asked.
The first hard frost is Ringing-Wood Day, and the fellers go out. You could hear it from Hob's Knap: every trunk ringing as it came down, the whole valley chiming like a dropped tray of spoons.

When the eels go down the Flume, the year has turned. They go late in Firstfruit, one night only, and the whole of the river street comes out along the channel with lanterns, quiet, because the eels can hear. This year it is Harvestmonth and they have not gone. I have no sign for that. I have put it here so that whoever comes after me can tell me what it meant.

When the last field is cut and the sheaf goes up on the gate, light the fires. That was the law of my office. Long Down to the north, Hob's Knap east above the orchard, Ewe Barrow west on the old mound, and every flock on the hills comes down to the light. Nobody has lit them since the wool went into the Hedge.

SIGNS TAKEN FROM SHEEP. I have a whole page of these and no sheep. A ewe that will not lie down at dusk. A flock that bunches with its back to the west. A tup that stamps in the fold. I will keep the page. Tamar Farrant has brought eleven ewes and a tup up from the Coast, and I mean to watch them and see if they still know what my father's sheep knew.
SIGNS FOR THE NIGHT.
Fog lying in the bottoms at dusk: sound runs along it like water along a pipe. Keep the fold quiet and the dogs in.
Rooks going home early and saying nothing: something is moving in the woods. Bring the dogs in, and the children.
When the wind drops dead on the Downs at the dead hour and stays dropped, go indoors. Do not wait to see why. Say something to your dog on the way, and keep saying it until you are inside.
SIGNS I HAVE HEARD OF AND NEVER SEEN.
That the beacons on the Downs can be seen from the Organum. Rubbish.

That the oaks of the Reach will one day drop every leaf they have in a single night. My grandmother had it from hers. I have never seen an iron-bough bare in my life, and I hope whoever sees it has a fire lit.
That there was a winter once, a real one, before the Reach was the Reach.

My knees do the hills by looking at them now. I sit at Gideon's window in the Bellwether with the three hills in front of me and watch the weather come over the Long Down, the way my father watched it. It comes all the same. That is the sign I would leave you, if I could leave only one: whatever else has gone wrong, the weather still comes from the west, and you can still see it coming over the hill, and there is still time to light the fires.
notes: Canon/game: Phase 22 text (Absalom Rudd, the old beacon-keeper who lit the fold-fires forty back-ends running on Long Down, Hob's Knap and Ewe Barrow, shepherds' fires so flocks came down to the light, not lit since the wool went into the Hedge; his knees will not do the hills; Gideon Thrale's Bellwether reopened when Tamar Farrant came back with eleven Rust Coast ewes and a tup); Phase 20-21 Rulings (flocks went into the Hedge and were eaten); Vol VII 2 and 8 (the Reach dates by what is growing; month names Firstfruit, Harvestmonth; Frostmonth mild in the Reach until 419); Vol V 4 (the Root kept the cold out for ten thousand years, here only as 'kept warm from underneath'); Series Bible Part III and IV (everyone over thirty remembers when red was redder; since 412 dogs howl at noon and milk sours overnight); Vol VII (b) (Ringing-Wood Day at the first hard frost; the Eel-Run late in Firstfruit, kept quiet because the eels can hear, and in 419 running late inside Harvestmonth; the sheaf on the gate); Series Bible Part VI (the oaks ring when the wind moves them). The leaf-falling legend is a folk rumour that foreshadows the Leaf-Fall of 18 Frostmonth 419 (Vol V) without stating it.
